opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question. The way I think about it is that test-time compute helps most when there's a real gap between generating an answer and verifying it. If checking a solution is a lot easier than coming up with one, then giving the model more time to think, to try different approaches, back up when something isn't working, and check its own work, pays off enormously. Math competitions, competitive programming, a lot of scientific reasoning problems fit that pattern, and that's where we've seen the most dramatic gains.

It actually goes back to my work on poker and Diplomacy. In poker, having the bot search and plan in real time, rather than just acting instantly from a precomputed policy, was worth more than scaling the model up by orders of magnitude. Seeing that again and again across games is what convinced me this would matter for language models too.

On the other side, there are tasks where thinking longer doesn't help much. If you ask what the capital of some country is, either the model knows it or it doesn't, and pondering for ten minutes won't change that. Knowledge retrieval, some creative writing, some subjective tasks where there isn't a clear notion of "more correct": those benefit less, at least right now.

That said, I'd caution people against drawing that line too firmly. A lot of things that look like pure recall or pure taste actually have a reasoning component once you dig into them. And as these models get better at things like planning, using tools, and checking their own outputs, I think the set of tasks that benefit from more thinking is going to keep growing. So rather than asking "which benchmarks benefit," I'd ask "where is the bottleneck reasoning versus raw knowledge," and increasingly the answer is reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says pondering longer will not change some factual answers, but does not state that performance on many factual-retrieval questions eventually plateaus as inference time increases.

r002.rationale: The response says factual retrieval benefits less and that pondering for ten minutes will not change a known-or-unknown answer; it does not say a little thinking can improve factual answers.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Sudoku or random search for constraint-satisfying assignments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about it is: which tasks actually have a verifiable answer, or at least a way to check your work? Because that's really where test-time compute shines. If you think about something like a math competition, AIME or the IMO, or a competitive programming problem, there's a clear notion of right and wrong, and more importantly, the model can reason for a while, try an approach, notice it's not working, back up, and try something else. That whole loop of generating candidates and critiquing them is what you're buying when you spend more compute at inference time. And on those benchmarks, the scaling curves are really clean. You give the model ten times more thinking time and it just gets better, pretty much log-linearly.

Where it helps a lot less is on things that are basically knowledge retrieval. If you ask a model who was the mayor of some city in 1870, no amount of thinking is going to help if it doesn't know. It's not a reasoning problem. So benchmarks that are mostly about recall, or about having seen the right fact in pretraining, you're not going to see big gains from test-time compute.

The thing I'd push back on, though, is the idea that this is just a math and code thing. That was the early story because those were the domains where it was easiest to train on and easiest to measure. But if you look at what's happened, the gains have carried over into harder-to-verify areas, scientific reasoning, legal analysis, writing that requires actually holding a complicated argument together. The common thread is that the task rewards thinking carefully before committing to an answer. Whether or not there's a clean grader, if a smart person would benefit from twenty minutes of thought instead of twenty seconds, the model probably does too.

And honestly, the thing I find most interesting is that a lot of existing benchmarks were designed around the assumption that models respond instantly. So they saturate fast once you add reasoning. The benchmarks that stay interesting are the ones where even an expert human needs real time, hours or days, and we're only starting to build those. That's where I think the field should be putting its evaluation effort.

r001.rationale: The response says extra thinking helps little with knowledge retrieval, especially when the model lacks the fact, but does not clearly state that performance on many factual-retrieval questions eventually plateaus as inference time increases.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that a little thinking improves factual-retrieval answers; it says thinking will not help when the model does not know the fact.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss Sudoku or random search over assignments satisfying its constraints.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: if you gave a person more time to think about the problem, would they do better? For something like a difficult math problem or a coding problem, the answer is usually yes. You can try an approach, discover that it doesn’t work, backtrack, and check your answer. Those are tasks where I’d expect more test-time compute to help.

If the question is asking for some obscure fact that you either know or don’t know, spending more time thinking may not help much. You need additional information, not necessarily additional reasoning.

There’s also the question of whether the benchmark has enough headroom. If a model already gets almost everything right with a quick response, it won’t tell you much about the value of thinking longer. So I’m particularly interested in difficult tasks where there’s a way to check progress or verify a solution, and where trying different approaches can actually change the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says extra thinking may not help with obscure facts, but does not state that performance on many factual-retrieval questions eventually plateaus as inference time increases.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a little extra thinking improves factual-retrieval answers; it says extra thinking may not help much when information is missing.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Sudoku or random search over assignments satisfying its constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether there’s something useful for the model to do with that additional compute. Can it explore different approaches, catch mistakes, and improve its answer? Math and coding are natural examples, because you can make progress toward a solution and often check whether it works.

If the benchmark is asking for some obscure fact, thinking longer may not help very much. You either have the information or you don’t. But if it’s asking you to reason through a problem, then there’s a much stronger case for spending more compute at test time.

And you have to look at the difficulty of the benchmark relative to the model. If the model already gets everything right, you won’t see a benefit. If the problems are completely beyond its capabilities, more thinking might not get you anywhere either. The interesting regime is where the model can solve the problem, but needs time to work through it.
